utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you. Good afternoon also to Banja Luka. Unfortunately, Madam Dahuron, we have to wait a second with the start. There is something that has priority, but let's first call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, this is Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And the appearances please for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Nicholas Koumjian, Ann Sutherland, and Ruth Karper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good to see you again hoping you are fit. For the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Branko Lukic for the Defence today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Before we start, we have to take the necessary arrangements, it's already Friday, for next week. Previously we heard, already in deviation of our order, that four witnesses would be called next week by the Defence. We received the amended proffer for Witness Number 006. Unfortunately, only an hour ago I learned from the Victim and Witness Unit that no additional witness would be called next week they don't -- wouldn't have any names or coordinates and would nothing -- would know nothing about the witnesses to come next week. May I hear the submission of the Defence related to this problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we have a written submission, so I haven't delivered it yet. If the usher could be so kind...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The problem, no doubt, is that as we had it previously when the Witness and Victims Unit has the correct coordinates only late, then this could create an obstacle for hearing the witnesses. And you yourself mentioned the problems with the necessary visa. Can you give us some additional hints related to witness 055, 083, 043 in order that the Victim and Witness Unit can prepare the necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. In this written submission, we tried to explain that -- and I think that the Court is aware of our efforts to locate Mr. -- actually the Witness Number 055. And if we are -- we do not locate him successfully by the next week, we'll withdraw this witness from our list of the witnesses. Witness Number 083 is still waiting for the permission of his superiors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And 043?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 043 is issued the passport, or should be issued the passport yesterday or today, as I was informed. So we will try to solve his visa problem at the beginning of the next week. And we are aware that we create problems for the Victim and Witness Unit, but that's only an additional burden on us because we accepted to transport our witnesses from the airport, to the airport. But these problems are really out of hands right now. We cannot solve them differently other than accepting to transport our witnesses back and forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would there be an additional witness available for the end of next week?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Hopefully, Your Honour, some of these remaining three witnesses should be with us the next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: As you mentioned yourself, granting a visa takes five days. How can you believe that when you start the request for obtaining such a visa only by Monday that Witness 043 could obtain the necessary visa during the next week and at the same time arrive in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Because with the assistance of the Victims and Witness Unit, we were able previously to speed up now this process. And if it's urgent, we learned that it can take only two or three days. Previously we were warned that it takes five days. Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask you to contact during the break the Witness and Victims Unit in order to give the necessary outstanding coordinates to the unit, that they at least can prepare the necessary in case there is no obstacle such as a nonpermission of the superior or the nonobtaining of the visa. Because it's Friday and it's really the last minute and the last possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I hear some submissions on this issue by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we simply hope the Defence is going to hold by its position to finish the case on time, because we're running out of time with the two additional Court-called witnesses, the expert witnesses, and we only have three more weeks before the end of the Defence case. If possible, if the Defence could give us when they can an indication of the remaining witnesses and the approximate order in which they --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We have to come back to this. It's planned when we have heard the witness via videolink. But absolute priority has to hear the Defence witnesses, but I would ask the legal officer of the Trial Chamber to start the emergency programme as soon as possible. I'll come back to this issue later, what it means "emergency programme." So we shouldn't waste the time and come back to you, Madam Dahuron. The usual sound check. Can you hear us?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Banja Luka] I can hear you perfectly. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It's a little bit difficult, but normally it improves. In the meantime, could we see the entire office and could you at the same time, please, escort the witness into your office. Thank you. [Witness testified through videolink].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good afternoon in Banja Luka. Can you hear me in a language you understand here from The Hague?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, yes, I can hear you and understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for coming. And may I please ask you to give us your solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this. You may be seated, please. Before we start the examination as such, may I ask you, you're aware that we are in public session now. Do you need any protective measures?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then as to the fact that you have been called as a Defence witness, the floor is yours, Mr. Lukic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Lukic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you know, my name is Branko Lukic and along with John Ostojic I represent Dr. Stakic before this Tribunal. Will you, please, for the record, give us your full name?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: Physician Slavica Popovic Radic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you tell us your father's name.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: Dusan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you born, Dr. Popovic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: 2nd of July, 1960.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were you born?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: In Omarska. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where do you live now?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: In Omarska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you tell us your occupation.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: I'm a physician, an MD, and I specialise in pediatrics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When and where did you graduate?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: I graduated from the school of medicine in Zagreb in 1985.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you tell us if you are married and whether you have any children?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: I am married. I have one child.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Between 1990 to 1993, were you a member of a political party?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you a member of a political party now?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: Now, I am a member of the democratic people's alliance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you tell us, after your graduation, where was your first job?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: After I graduated, I was duty-bound to return to Omarska because I had there a scholarship, so that I was an intern in the general hospital, or rather the health centre in Prijedor, and the clinical centre in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you enroll in your specialisation course?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long did it take?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: Well, the first part of my specialisation training lasted until 1992. That is, until the conflict broke out. And then I was asked to come back because we were under a labour obligation in Omarska. After a while, I was allowed to continue with my specialisation training.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you were summoned for your labour obligation, you did that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: Had I not done that within five days, I would have lost my job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever work together with Dr. Milomir Stakic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, as of the moment when Dr. Milomir Stakic came to work for our health institution, 1989, and for a part of 1990, that is, until I went to start my specialisation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you tell us, what was the situation in your health institution in Omarska at the time when you came to do -- when you came to discharge your labour obligation? I mean medical supplies mostly.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: The situation in the health institution in Omarska was very difficult. Until then, there were sufficient personnel, both doctors, paramedics and all the auxiliary personnel so that we could provide adequate health protection to the civilian population around our centre. However, a few months before I was summoned to come back medicines from Prijedor from the central pharmacy, which supplied our health centre pharmacy in Omarska, these medicines practically stopped arriving or arrived in very small quantities so that our stocks of, be it medicines or any other medical supplies, bandages and so on and so forth, were drastically reduced.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from the shortage of medicines, what about other medical supplies?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: The same. There was a shortage of the medical supplies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, were there also power outages?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So how did your institution operate during power cuts?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: At that time, when there would be no electricity, we could not work simply we could not perform even elementary laboratory tests. We had no electricity. The only solution, the only possible solution was to accord priority to our health institution which meant that we would be allowed to get our electricity via a generator.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to get the electricity in such a manner, did it mean that you had to buy oil or some fuel for these generators, and how did you do that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: Well, we had to get the diesel since we were on the priority list, and people were aware of the importance of health care and health institution, the army allowed -- helped us to get the necessary fuel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you and when become a member of Kolo Srpskih Sestara --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's comment, the charity organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And will you tell us what its task was?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: When the investigation centre in Omarska was founded, we needed medicines and medical supplies. And one of the priority tasks of the Kolo Srpskih Sestara and doctors, and I was one of the founding members of this humanitarian organisation which was founded with the help of the orthodox church, and there together with Dobrotvor cooperated with Caritas, which is a Catholic humanitarian organisation, and Merhamet, which is the Muslims' humanitarian organisation, our chief priority was to ensure the supply of medicines from abroad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were your efforts successful, and how many medicines did you get from abroad and from whom?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: Well, the effort invested was tremendous because on the one hand you have a population with an increasing need for health care, the ever-decreasing medicine supplies, so we usually approached our citizens working abroad, and they sent us medicines. Often not adequately packaged or stored, which because of long delays at the borders and very high temperatures, frequently could not be used any longer once they reached us. The army tried to help, and they gave us medicines and the necessary medical supplies in quantities that they could afford.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know when did the conflict in Kozarac break out, and what happened that day in relation to your institution?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: Towards the end of April, I think. Was it April, May 1992? I'm not quite sure. I'm not sure about the date. But whatever. The conflict commenced. The first one was brought, but he died shortly afterwards. I believe his name was Zeljko Zgonjanin. All the available medical personnel from the area of Omarska were invited to the health centre because we were anticipating a large -- a considerable number of wounded and killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let's see this first. When this killed soldier, and you tell us his name is Zeljko Zgonjanin, when he was brought to your medical institution, were you on duty at the time or were you at home?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: I was there, I was working because I had been on duty the previous night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after this soldier was brought, did you invite -- did you ask the other personnel to come before or after the soldier was brought?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: After he was brought.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the conflict in Kozarac, were all the wounded brought to your medical establishment or only some, and if so, which ones?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: Because of our ability or the potential we had to offer medical assistance, we only had lightly wounded people brought to us. The more serious cases were sent to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the conflict in Kozarac was over, did people from Kozarac come to Omarska; and if so, how did they come, and can you explain that to us?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: After the conflict was over, people were brought in buses in front of the hall of culture in Omarska, there were many acquaintances amongst them, friends. People were bringing, food, water, whatever they had, in order to make the situation of these people a little easier, the situation that they found themselves in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what the structure of the people was who were in those buses, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: Children, women, and there were elderly men on board.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened to these people? Did they stay in Omarska or did they continue on their way?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: They didn't stay in Omarska. They went on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who transported those people?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the building of the medical centre, or the Omarska clinic, did Dr. Gajic, Slobodan, work there?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: Not in the first few days after the outbreak of the conflict. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. After a few days, Dr. Slobodan Gajic came. He was a mobilised soldier. And he said that he would be providing medical services to the detainees in the investigation centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Gajic, was he a civilian or a soldier?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: A soldier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how often Dr. Gajic went to the Omarska investigation centre?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: He went every day, usually in the morning. If necessary, he also went in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Dr. Gajic also sleep at the medical centre?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did. One of the rooms in the medical centre was given to him as a room where he could sleep so that he was also available 24 hours a day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Other than the fact that he slept there, was Dr. Gajic also somebody who was a part of the medical centre, or was he just a member of the army?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: He was not a part of the medical centre. He didn't actually provide medical assistance there. He was a member of the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Dr. Gajic did not provide medical assistance to people in the -- on the premises of your medical centre?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: No, this was done by our doctors and by our medical staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were prisoners brought from the Omarska investigation centre to the medical centre?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: Yes, this did happen. In urgent cases, patients were brought -- patients who had asthma attacks, difficulties breathing, or who had some kind of kidney failure or high temperature. There were also some lightly wounded cases while I was on duty. One gunshot wound. That wounded person was somebody that I had sent for further surgical treatment to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there people who had sustained beating injuries?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: There were bruises, but mostly I saw people who had the usual health problems, the ones that I mentioned, difficulties with breathing and kidney attacks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see anyone from the Omarska investigation centre who had fractured bones?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that the person with the gunshot wound was sent for further treatment to Banja Luka. You did that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you need any approval from anybody in order to do that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: After primary care of the wound, I had to seek approval in order to send the patient for further medical treatment. I called the police station in Omarska so that they would contact the investigation centre and ask whether I would be allowed to send the patient for further medical treatment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you personally were not able to directly contact the Omarska investigation centre?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a Crisis Staff in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever receive any instructions from the Crisis Staff relating to ill persons who were brought from the Omarska investigation centre?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, did you provide medical assistance at the same time to the population of Omarska and the neighbouring villages?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: Yes, this was implied. We continuously provided medical assistance to the population under extremely difficult circumstances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your colleagues, were they mobilised at the time and sent on duty outside of your medical centre?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: My colleagues, men, were very quickly mobilised and sent to the front. At one point, one doctor, a woman doctor, was also mobilised so that there were only us two women doctors who remained at the medical centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please be so kind and tell us the name of that woman doctor who was mobilised at that time.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: Her name was Dr. Brankica Rosic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you treat in the same way the people that were brought from the Omarska investigation centre like the regular patients who came to the medical centre?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: Absolutely the same way, perhaps with even more attention because of the place where they happened to be at that time. We provided assistance to them and gave them medicines that we were not able to offer to the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anyone ever tell you not to extend medical assistance to people brought from the investigation centre or to give them lesser quality care than provided to the other patients who came to your medical institution?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: Nobody ever told us that. The doctors have their code of conduct and their ethics, and they know what they are supposed to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who brought the wounded from the Omarska investigation centre to your medical institution?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: Policemen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know these policemen?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: Some, yes; and some, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware that they were mostly reserve police officers, or were you not aware of that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember how long you were carrying out the work duty at the Omarska medical centre?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: For about a year and a half.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever leave the territory of Republika Srpska and Bosnia and Herzegovina during the war?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: Yes, during the war, I left the territory only once, the territory of Republika Srpska of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I accompanied a patient who was taken to a clinic in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have to have some special passes for that trip?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: Yes, I had to have a movement permit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who obtained this permit for you when you accompanied this patient to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: I don't know who got that. The family, I think, of the patient who wanted me to accompany the patient obtained this permit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that you didn't apply for this permit yourself, but do you know which institution was the one to issue this permit in order to leave the territory of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: It was requested from the military department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: There's an objection on the part of the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, to relevance. First, we don't even know which year of the four or five years of war that we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would you please take this into account when putting the question to the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Popovic, you heard the objection from the Prosecution. Can you please tell us, if you remember, in which period did you accompany the patient to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: This was not at the beginning of the war. There was a corridor, and we were able to go to Belgrade. So perhaps this was then maybe in the third year. But I'm not sure. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the second part when we were talking about the patients from the Omarska investigation centre and we were talking about Dr. Gajic, I assumed that we were talking about the spring/summer of 1992.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When we came back -- since we're back talking about Dr. Gajic, can you please tell us if he shared his information with you? Did he tell you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. what was being done at the investigation centre? Was it his duty to provide any kind of a report to you or to your medical institution?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't have any duty or obligation to submit any kind of report to our institution. We didn't talk -- I mean, he didn't ever tell us anything about what was happening at the investigation centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say Dr. Gajic was available 24 hours a day.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is in theory, but those --

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: To the health, to the health centre in Omarska. The health centre in Omarska had an organised health service, an emergency service, regular doctors on duty. And they provided regular health assistance, both during the day and during the night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During these 24 hours that, as you say, Dr. Gajic was available whenever he was giving medical assistance to the injured and the wounded, he did that at the Omarska health centre and not at your institution. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: I've already said that. Medical assistance at our institution was provided by our doctors, those who were employed at the Omarska health centre and those who were available.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the conflict in Kozarac when soldier Zeljko Zgonjanin was killed, did you hear about the existence of a paramilitary formation called El Manijakosi, and did you hear what they were saying, what they said, after the death of this soldier?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: Towards the evening hours, a group of people arrived. They were armed, and they asked to see the soldier who was killed. When they were taken to the room where Zgonjanin, Zeljko, was lying in, they lit a candle, crossed themselves, and said "Don't be surprised if we want revenge, and we will have our revenge." And they called themselves Manijakosi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would now like to ask you something about Dr. Stakic, about your personal knowledge relating to your colleague. Could you please first tell us how long have you known Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: I've known Dr. Stakic since he was a student at the high school. He was one generation after me. Serious, quiet, a withdrawn student as well as an excellent student, an extremely good student. He comes from an honest and poor family. Later, when I left for my medical studies in Zagreb, he studied in Banja Luka, and we didn't see one another in that period during our studies. I would occasionally see him in Prijedor. When he began to work at our medical institution, he was a mature, educated doctor who approached his work in the best possible way. He performed his job conscientiously. The patients liked him very much. Because he was young and he only started his career, he was asked to work in local medical centres. He worked in Lamovita and Kevljani in the medical health centres there, and he also worked on duty a lot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us the ethnic composition of the population in these villages covered by Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: Gornja Lamovita has a mixed population. Besides Serbian patients, patients of other ethnic groups also came for medical treatment there. They were mostly Muslims. And in the health centre in Kevljani, which was in that local community, the population was Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how Dr. Stakic was regarded in Kevljani?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: I will give you just one example.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, if you remember, which year he worked in Kevljani.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: He began to work sometime in 1989, so that would be that year. 1989 to 1990, until the time I went off for my specialisation. So I don't know what happened after that. But during that period, when he worked there, he was a well-loved doctor in Kevljani. The people liked him and were satisfied with his work. There were never any complaints about his work. When we wanted to have some other doctors come and work at that infirmary, and I think there was a doctor who came after Dr. Stakic, Dr. Ekrem Hodzic, we wanted to make it possible for him also to be on duty at the infirmary for a while, so he could have that work experience there, too, along with Dr. Stakic. The people from Kevljani did not want that. The people from that local commune of Kevljani were extremely satisfied with the work of Dr. Stakic, so that he was the only doctor -- or the permanent doctor in that local commune.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This new doctor who was supposed to be working there, could you please tell us his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: Ekrem Hodzic, yes, Ekrem Hodzic was a Muslim by ethnicity. But he's a man who was not born in our region. He came there after he got married, and the people didn't know him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are from Omarska. Do you know which political party Dr. Stakic belonged to in 1990 and 1991?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: I know that he was the president of the people's radical party of Veljko Guberina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Working with Dr. Stakic, did you ever notice him showing any kind of hatred or intolerance towards other ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: No, never. His work and what he did were characterised by a professional expert approach, and he never differentiated amongst people on ethnic grounds.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In late 1992 or early 1993, did you hear that Dr. Stakic was replaced as president of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: Yes. We heard that he had been replaced.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know any details regarding this replacement?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: I don't know any details. We weren't all that interested in that at the time. Our role in all of that was different. We were fighting for our survival.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In regard to the Omarska investigation centre, I must ask you if you ever went there to provide medical assistance to the prisoners in the investigation centre itself.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before Dr. Gajic came, who, as you said, was a soldier and was mobilised and who worked at the investigation centre Omarska and provided medical assistance to the detainees there, did any of your colleagues go to the investigation centre to provide medical assistance?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: As soon as the centre was formed, my colleagues went there, together with other medical staff, and they provided medical assistance, and they examined those who said that they needed medical assistance. And then they went on the second day, so they actually went there on the two days before Dr. Gajic's arrival.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We mentioned the Crisis Staff that was operating in Omarska. Do you know what the powers and the functions of this Crisis Staff were?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, were you aware of the existence of the Crisis Staff of the Prijedor Municipal Assembly? Did you hear about that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: Well, one could assume there was one such Crisis Staff, since there was also an Omarska one, but I didn't know much about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know what its competencies would be?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Popovic. This concludes our direct examination. And now, you will be asked questions by our learned friends from the Prosecution and Their Honours. Thank you very much once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. The Prosecution is prepared for immediate start of the cross?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. The questions will now be put to you by Mr. Koumjian representing the Office of the Prosecutor. Cross-examined by Mr. Koumjian:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, you talked about doing an internship, and Dr. Stakic doing an internship as part of your medical training. Can you explain to us what this internship would consist of in Prijedor at the time that -- well, let's say that at the time Dr. Stakic did it, in 1989? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: No, I did not say that. After I finished the school of medicine in Zagreb in 1985, I was duty-bound to do my internship lasting one year. And I did that in the general hospital in Prijedor, that is, the emergency service of the health centre in Prijedor and in the Banja Luka hospital. And after my one-year internship, I went on working for the health centre in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, madam. You misunderstood my question, and perhaps I wasn't clear. First, and let me ask you, when did Dr. Stakic do his internship, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: Dr. Stakic came to us in 1989, and I believe that he had already finished his internship because before that, he had worked in Teslic, I believe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When Dr. Stakic, you said, came to you, where do you mean that he was working at the time, from 1989 until the -- through 1992? Where did he work?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: In 1989, he got a job with the health centre in Omarska and became a full-time employee of the health centre. One of his tasks was the emergency service, then duty, and also field practice in two clinics, in two infirmaries, in Donja Lamovita and Kevljani. In 1990, sometime in spring, I went for my specialisation to Banja Luka, and Dr. Stakic stayed behind at the Omarska health centre. And I think that in early 1991, he went to become the deputy president of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor, and thus stopped working for the health centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain to us, would it be correct that the Omarska health centre was a primary-care facility and that for those with more serious or more complicated conditions, they were referred to the Prijedor or Banja Luka health centres. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: You mean the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: Or the detainees? The civilian population, I see. The health centre provides primary care. The secondary care is provided by the general hospital in Prijedor, and above them is the Banja Luka centre. What could not be done at our level, we would first send our patients to Prijedor to the general hospital, and if the cases were too difficult, too complicated for them, those were sent to Banja Luka to the clinical centre there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the case of a young doctor with relatively little experience, is it common for those doctors to interact with more experienced colleagues and more specialised colleagues in the treatment of patients?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: Well, every physician in a health centre has his surgery, his room, where he works, in which he examines and treats patients. But every morning, after -- when people have come to work, there are consultations, and the doctor on duty reports on the developments during the night when experienced his exchange naturally with senior colleagues. And younger colleagues who had come to work could, after internship, also ask for help if necessary, to be helped in case of either establishing diagnosis or treating more serious, more complicated cases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be common, for example, for a general practitioner, as I gather those at the health centre like Dr. Stakic were, to confer with specialists such as cardiologists, gynecologists, obstetricians, ear, nose, and throat specialists, those type of specialists regarding conditions that they encounter in their patients?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: As part of the primary health care in our medical centre in Omarska, we had a consultation specialised service, and this was provided by three specialists, gynecologist, internist, and pediatrician. These doctors worked once a week. All patients during the day and during the previous week were sent to them if their expert opinion was felt to be required. If the patient's condition demanded it, the general practitioner would send these patients for examinations to the appropriate specialists.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When a patient is referred by the general practitioner to a specialist, is it common for them to give the specialist the background of the patient, to brief them regarding what was discovered in the initial examination by the general practitioner?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: A general practitioner, in his daily work, examines the patient in detail, performs all the necessary laboratory tests. And only then, after the general practitioner has concluded that that particular health institution cannot provide the necessary treatment, he then asks for consultation and for the examination of that patient and refers the patient to the specialist. And the patient takes with him his whole case history, the test results, and everything else, he takes to that other doctor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your experience observing Dr. Stakic, did he have relations -- tend to have relations with only Serb doctors, or did he have relationships with doctors of non-Serbian ethnicity, particularly Muslim and Croat doctors?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: In our health institution at that time, before me and Dr. Stakic, for years Dr. Angela Mladenova had worked there. She is Bulgarian, and there were also two Muslims, a couple, who worked there. There was no difference, any in our communication, because of our different ethnic origins. Nobody, and that includes Dr. Stakic, ever discriminated between the colleagues on the basis of their ethnic origin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not asking about who was at the clinic before you and Dr. Stakic arrived. But did Dr. Stakic interact with Muslims and Croat doctors in Prijedor Municipality? Was this -- was the community of doctors in Prijedor small enough that you knew each other and interacted with each other?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: Well, we all knew one another since there were not so many doctors, so that we all knew one another. I don't know whether he was friends with somebody and who. But I suppose there was no reason why not to have such friends. We were all friends, be it at professional meetings, workshops, lectures. There was no difference between us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it common for doctors to attend, you mentioned workshops, lectures, different aspects of what we would call in my profession continuing education, and were there social events where doctors in Prijedor of all ethnicities would get together?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: At the education, the continuing education, yes, that goes on. And that is why we attended workshop and seminars and lectures before the war and now. There were also other types of get togethers, either marking anniversaries of the health centre, or there was the nurses' day or physicians' day, the 8th of March.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam, without giving me the address, can you just tell me in 1992, at the outbreak of the conflict, in what area did you live? Did you live in the town, in Omarska? Where did you live?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: At that time, I was undergoing my specialisation in Banja Luka. And I lived there part time. I usually commuted by car from work to Omarska where my home was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your home was in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't have my house in Banja Luka. I was staying with some friends in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Where was your house, in what area?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: My house, the flat that I live in, is in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And in 1992 when the -- let's say when the -- would you call it the conflict in Kozarac broke out, were you staying at your flat in Omarska or where were you at that time?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: In the very early days of the conflict, my assignments were such that that night, I was on duty at the Omarska health centre. And I stayed there in the infirmary during the day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From your location, could you see the army shelling the Kozarac area, the area of Kozarac, Kevljani, and places like that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: The only thing I saw were the patients in front of me. And it was so traumatic, it was so hard on us when wounded and killed started to arrive that physicians never left the infirmaries, the clinics, the bandaging centres, bandaging rooms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you mentioned one person, and I'm sorry, I've forgotten his Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. last name, but Zeljko Zgonjanin, I believe. And would it be correct that he was a soldier of Serbian ethnicity who was killed. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: It is. He was the first soldier, young. He had an entry/exit wound in the kidney area. We remember him because he was the first man to be brought there, the first man who died before our eyes of such a wound.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, madam, before this soldier was brought in, the area had been shelled for approximately two days. Is that correct? Had you seen any patients before that time?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned the horror of seeing people brought --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: From the testimony of this witness, it is not clear when this killed soldier was brought in. And I think that the Prosecution should first establish that moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Fair enough. I don't think the Prosecution will have no problems with adding the concrete date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, do you remember that the soldier was brought in, would it be correct, on Tuesday, the 26th of May, and that the shelling of the Kozarac area had begun on Sunday, the 24th of May?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: I mean, I can't. I can tell you it was in the beginning of the conflict, so it was late May. But I don't know the exact date. When the conflict started, that is when this soldier was brought to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, isn't it correct that there was artillery fire for two days before the soldier was brought in. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, did you treat any victims of shelling?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any children brought to your clinic who had been wounded by artillery shells, mortars, and tank fire?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: No. No. No, no such children came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anyone make you aware that Dr. Idriz Merdzanic had been asking for an ambulance to evacuate two dying children from the area of Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I don't know which doctor asked for it. But whatever the case, we received an application to send an ambulance to Kozarac. Two nurses went there and a driver. So the ambulance car was sent. But they returned shortly afterwards frightened, and they were shouting at the doctor who had sent them because they had been exposed to gunfire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, you mentioned the area, the village of Kevljani, where you stayed Dr. Stakic was well loved. Did you see that area of Kevljani after the 26th of May, after the shelling of the army?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware that all of the people of Kevljani were forced from their homes during that attack, many of their homes were burned down, and many of them were taken to the Omarska, Keraterm, and Trnopolje camps?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: I don't know. One could assume, after the conflict, that a number of their houses were destroyed. The majority -- the majority of the population were brought in buses, women, children, were brought to the cultural centre in Omarska. As for other investigation centres apart from Omarska, no, I didn't learn about them straight away. I learned about Trnopolje later on. It was said that there were people there, and that they could go out and come in freely, that they were best protected there so that nobody would harm them or harass them in any way. As for Keraterm, no, I did not hear about it for a long time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, do you know if anything that Dr. Stakic did for the people of Kevljani who had suffered this attack and then were put on those buses? Can you tell us anything specifically that you know Dr. Stakic did for them?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, did you treat women prisoners at the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: Well, they were my patients at our health centre. I had a female patient who -- with a fever and some urinary tract infection. And then another female patient, or rather a woman who usually came with them, and I saw her in silk track suit. So she stood apart from the others in a way. Those female patients were extended medical aid. They were given a drip feed, antibiotics, and their treatment continued in the investigation centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, can we go into private session for a few minutes. I see we're about to break. Is that correct? We're going to break at quarter ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Private session is enough?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, you talked about a Dr. Gajic going to the Omarska camp. Did you send him to that camp?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: No. Dr. Gajic came as a soldier, said he'd been called up, and that as of that moment, he'd take care of the health of the detainees in the investigation centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Madam, I'm going to read for you now some testimony by a Slobodan Gajic during a different case. And for counsel, it's page 11.672 of the Kvocka case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We object, Your Honour. It's -- we were not allowed during the Prosecution case to present any witness with a statement of some other witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We discussed it previously. Let's have the break for the videolink now for the next 30 minutes, and let's discuss this procedural issue, please, in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can you hear us in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Koumjian, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we do have some transcripts to hand out to the Court and counsel. I guess we only have one transcript -- we do have three for the Court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, madam, you talked about Dr. Gajic. Dr. Gajic actually came from Jajce. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: He came, introduced himself, said he was a doctor, a soldier, or actually that he was a doctor who was mobilised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. He was not from Prijedor. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. He wasn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, I'm going to put to you some testimony of Mr. Gajic on page 11.693 beginning on line 16. Madam, Dr. Gajic testified in other case, and he was asked by a Judge Rodrigues, "Did you have can I say a calendar of your present -- of the presence of each doctor a schedule or did the physicians all arrive at the same time or did they have a schedule according to which they would go to the centre?" And he answer: "Dr. Slavica Popovic was the head administrator of the health centre, and she would determine the scheduling and order in which the doctors visited." Judge Rodrigues asked: "Okay, so you were there you went to the centre on the basis of instructions received by Dr. Slavica Popovic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please read slowly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your answer was: "The first morning visit we knew that's what we had to do first and that as soon as we got up we would go to that first visit --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you please slow down. The interpreters can't follow.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the text perhaps be put on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We don't have an extra copy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The answer on page 11.694 at the top, the top of 11.694, please. The answer of Dr. Gajic was: "The first morning, we knew that's what we had to do first. And then as soon as we got up, we would go to that first visit. So for that first visit, we didn't need an order or an indication from anybody. We knew that was our job. As soon as we got all the medicines we needed, we would go straight to the centre for the morning visit. "As for the other visits, they would be done on the basis of phone calls. If we were phoned up or if Dr. Slavica told us to go there, we would go." Then earlier, on page 11.672, beginning on line 4 - it is 11.672 - Dr. Gajic was asked on line 4: "Could you please explain to the Tribunal what arrangements you made with the lady doctor, and what she -- how she told you to cover the health centre -- why she told you to cover the health centre?" And Dr. Gajic answered: "She told me to cover the centre because I am from a different region. I come from a different area, and I didn't know the people who were in the investigation centre." Madam, did you tell Dr. Gajic to go to the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: Dr. Gajic, as I said, was mobilised. He was a soldier and a doctor who said that he came there together with the driver and the military ambulance and that he would, from now on, be providing medical treatment at the investigation centre. Myself, I myself, or any other doctor were not able to tell anything to Dr. Slobodan Gajic. He took over the work at the investigation centre while we carried out with our daily duties. We continuously provided medical assistance at the medical centre. As far as the duty rote, I don't know why he picked me. I wasn't the one who was making the decisions about who would be on duty because already, at the beginning of the conflict, we all had a meeting and had an internal agreement about which doctors would be on duty. Two doctors were on duty every night. So none of us were present at the infirmary around the clock. So it wasn't possible for us to tell him when he would go, because -- and when it was necessary for him to go because he was present at the health centre every day while none of us were there every day. And there was another third thing that he said. Could you please repeat that for me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, isn't it a fact you told him to go to the camp, that he would be appropriate because he was not from Prijedor and did not know the detainees?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: I did not -- I was in no position to send anyone or to decide who would go to the investigation centre. I've already said earlier that we did not have any telephone communication with them. If there was a need for any medical treatment at the investigation centre, then the police station informed us either by telephone or they would come personally requesting that medical help be sent to the investigation centre. We didn't keep any records of that. We were a civilian health centre in charge of the health of the civilian population. When there was need for us to give medical assistance to the detainees at the investigation centre, then we would also do that. And possibly, there are records about those prisoners, patients who were given medical treatment at the medical centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, madam, on the basis of these phone calls you're talking about, do you now admit that you went to the Omarska camp when detainees were present?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't understand each other. Dr. Gajic Slobodan would go, but if there was any need for medical assistance, after we were contacted by the police station or the policemen came, then our vehicle would go to bring the prisoners to the clinic where we would give them medical assistance. Sometimes the police themselves would use their own vehicles to bring the prisoners from the investigation centre to the clinic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, one time, so I'm absolutely clear I understand you: Were you ever in the Omarska camp when detainees were present?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 11.686 of the transcript of Mr. Gajic - perhaps the usher could put it on the ELMO, it's a short question and answer - Judge Riad asked the doctor, beginning on line 1: "This pressure, because you were the only man, the only doctor for all the camp?" And Dr. Gajic answered: "No, other doctors visited the camp, including Slavica Popovic, Nada Ljubic, Jasenka Mijatovic, and Vlado Radic, and others whom I don't remember because I had already gone. But I was the one who went there the most. I was the regular one." Madam, do you still deny going to the camp?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: I've said that the doctors at the clinic gave medical assistance to the investigation centre during those first few days until Dr. Slobodan Gajic was mobilised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, then, now do I understand you to say that you did go to the camp before Dr. Gajic went to the camp?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever been -- madam --

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: I didn't go. During those days, other doctors went there. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, do you know someone named Ljubian Andzic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: I know him. He's from the same place. He had many acquaintances and friends at the investigation centre, and he went to the centre often. He took medicines there, food, and whatever else was needed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, did Dr. -- did Ljubjan Andzic, was he a medical technician who was sent to the Omarska camp, not as a detainee but sent there as a medical professional?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: Yes, he's a medical technician, and he did go in the capacity of nurse. But then he also, because of his connections and the large number of acquaintances and friends, he also went privately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, you went to the Omarska camp with Mr. Andzic. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: No. I did set out to go. There were some interventions. They asked that all available medical staff go to the Omarska investigation centre. But at some point, once we had passed the gate but before actually getting into the centre, we were all turned back because there was a man who was wounded who was of Serbian ethnicity, and then another one of Muslim ethnicity, and nobody else had remained at the medical centre. We had to go back. But since the people who had been wounded inside the investigation centre had already been taken care of and given assistance, there was no need for us to go there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I interrupt for procedural reasons. May I ask you, based on the fact that apparently you are an important witness for this case, and it seems to be not sufficient to hear you by videolink only, what would be a possible date for you to come to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For personal reasons, I cannot come to The Hague, and that is why, after talking with the lawyers, I decided to testify by videolink. I have a small child that I'm not able to leave in the care of anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You have relatives? And how old is your child?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My child is 6 years old. It was never separated from me until now. At the moment, I'm living by myself with my son. And the closest relative that I have is my mother. She is 73 years old, and she is ill and unable to take care of my child.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber will have to decide later whether it's mandatory to hear you as a live witness, because no doubt, the probative value of a videolink testimony is a lower one than that of a live witness. Please take this into account when answering the following questions, and I would ask the Prosecution to repeat the last question once more.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I believe she did answer that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But, madam, is it true that you went to the Omarska camp with Mr. Ljubjan Andzic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: I think that I've already given an answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you enter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry. But the end of the answer was: "But there was no need for us to go there." This is your final answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, we went there because they said that all available medical personnel should be placed at the disposal of the investigation centre. But by the time we got there, Dr. Gajic and the nurse I think -- or the nurse, Ljuban Andzic, I think he went with us, he went inside, and we were told that the patients had already been taken care of, and that we should go back to the clinic because two wounded persons had been sent there. One of Serb ethnicity and one of Muslim ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, madam --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'd like to have another transcript distributed. I'm sorry, but we only have three copies. So perhaps, one for the ELMO, one for the Judges, and one for the Defence. I'd like to have page 7.535, the bottom line, put on the ELMO, and then the top of the next page.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, Mr. Ljubjan Andzic testified in front of this Tribunal under oath on the 7th of February, 2002. Let me check the year. 2001, excuse me. And he was asked: "Was there any doctor at the medical centre in Omarska who would go there with you?" Referring to the camp. And his answer was: "Dr. Slavica Popovic would go." Do you know of any reason why Mr. Andzic would believe or say that you had gone to the camp with him?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: I told you that during shooting in the camp itself at the investigation centre when all available medical staff was called, I went in that group to the investigation centre, in the group of medical personnel. I was never there with Ljuban Andzic. I believe that at that -- that one time, Ljuban Andzic was one of the medical personnel at the investigation centre, but I never went with him. Our doctors provided medical assistance there only in the first few days after the establishment of the investigation centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, did you ever treat Professor Muhamed Cehajic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: Do you mean during the war, Professor Muhamed Cehajic?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever treat Professor Muhamed Cehajic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: I didn't have the opportunity before the war. During the war, during the visit of a part of the team which was to investigate the possibilities of providing the most efficient health service to the detainees at the investigation centre, I saw Muhamed Cehajic on that occasion. He was examined by another doctor and prescribed treatment for him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was Professor Cehajic when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: Then, when I saw him, he was at the investigation centre, and he was at the clinic which was allocated as the place where patients would be treated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, can you describe where this clinic was in the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: It was one room. It wasn't a real clinic. It was a room which had been allocated for examinations and for the prescribing of therapy, of treatment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which building was it in?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: It wasn't a building. It was a rather low house, a rather low room. Around it were buildings, and that was a rather low room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, when you saw Professor Cehajic, who else was present?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: There was another colleague who attended the same secondary school as I did in Prijedor. Professor Cehajic was our teacher. He taught us Serbo-Croatian, and there were also two female nurses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the colleague that you attended school with?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: Dr. Vlado Radic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, I'm going to have a diagram - Mr. Usher, please - put on the screen to look at. It's S15-18. And I realise this may be difficult because you can't point -- we can't see you pointing here. But looking at this diagram, you'll see several buildings, one is a white house to the bottom right, and then there are larger buildings, one at the top right and one to the left. Where was the clinic that you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: Oh, dear. Why it was such a fleeting moment. I don't know. That white one. What is this room behind those buildings? This low, lower room, but I'm not sure. I know that that room wasn't part of the buildings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you believe it was in this white house that you saw Professor Cehajic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: In that room, he applied for examination. I think it is that room, but I'm not sure. All I know is that it wasn't part of these large buildings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, can you tell us what you observed about the condition of the mayor -- excuse me, the president of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor, Muhamed Cehajic, when you saw him on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: Well, he was upset. He was distraught. He asked to be examined, to have his heart examined, because earlier on, he used to have a heart complaint. He said he had had a cardiac infarction, and he asked to be given some tranquiliser and some painkiller.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see evidence that he had been beaten?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: Well, when he pulled his shirt up, one could see a bruise on his back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you he was urinating blood?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, do you know why Professor Cehajic was detained in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, did you know colleagues of yours, doctors, who were detained at the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: Well, we heard that some of them were in the centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, I'd like to go to private session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: Well, Dr. Stakic was the president of the people's radical party of Veljko Guberina. Whether he was a member of any other party before that, I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Dr. Stakic, you told us, is it correct that he ran for office and elected as a deputy of the assembly in the 1990 elections and stopped practicing medicine in order to take up the position of vice-president of the municipality, is that correct, in 1991?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: What I know, that he was vice-president from the beginning of 1991. But at that time, I had absolutely no part in the political life, and I knew nothing of any nominations, elections, or whatever. And I wasn't interested in that at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In -- at the end of the war, in 1996, 1997, did Dr. Stakic return in 1996 as the president of the municipality and again give up the practice of medicine?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: I think that when Dr. Stakic left the Municipal Assembly, then he did not work directly as a doctor, as a physician, offering -- providing medical aid. When he was the director of the health centre, what were the years, I really don't know. I can't remember that exactly. But I do know he was the director of the health centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So as the director of the health centre, he would have been an administrator in charge of many other doctors but not himself providing care to patients. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I turn immediately to the line of questions put to you by Prosecution counsel. Could you please tell us the exact date when Dr. Slobodan Gajic arrived in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: I can't say the exact date. But I said it was shortly after the establishment, a few days later. That is when he came to the health centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: When would you fix the date of the establishment?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: After the establishment of what? I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I made reference to your own answer. When asked when Dr. Slobodan Gajic arrived in Omarska, you answered: "I can't say the exact date, but I said it was shortly after the establishment, a few days later." And therefore, my question was: Establishment of what?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't say exactly when the investigation centre was set up. But it was a few days after it was set up. I don't know exactly the date, but just a few days after it was established, after it was set up, he came.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would you, with the assistance of some important incidents that happened at that time, try to the best of your recollection be more precise on the date. And maybe it will help that I bring to your attention another part of Dr. Gajic's testimony on the 11th of May, 2001. Page 11.671 where he said: "And on the 25th of May, I reported to the military unit in Banja Luka and was mobilised into a brigade. That is to say, the health section, sanitary corps, medical corps of that brigade. It was the 1st Brigade, the 1st Armoured Brigade." And then later, line 24, it reads -- let's start with the next answer. When asked: "How did you organise your work in the Omarska health centre?" The answer of Dr. Gajic was: "In the Omarska health centre, work was organised in the following way: We catered to the civilian population, the military, and the police force. And the lady doctor -- I don't know at that time -- I didn't know - at that time informed me that an investigation centre had been set up and that I would have to do that work, too -- we would have to do that work, too." So does this assist you and refresh your recollection?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: I was asked as a doctor to help, as a doctor who is under work obligation. Other doctors, perhaps, have a better memory and remember better all those dates. Because after all, I went there to help them, to extend the best health care possible. That was my primary task. A lot of time has elapsed since those events. And it's a very painful experience about something that happened in our lands. I cannot give you the exact date when this investigation centre was set up. And Dr. Gajic - I'm sorry - at that time, when he came, I wasn't the head of that health centre. It was Dr. Nada Lukic who was at the head of the centre at the time, because the then director could not get to Omarska because of the barricades. So she could speak about the investigation centre, but he must have known about it because he was sent there. He as a doctor never treated -- never had anything to do with the civilian population in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: How long did Dr. Slobodan Gajic stay at Omarska, work in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure. I suppose as long as that investigation centre operated. People there could not be left without health care.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In the same testimony I mentioned before, on page 11.679, Dr. Gajic was asked: "Approximately when would you have been the last time that you went to the Omarska camp?" The answer was: "I cannot remember exactly when it was, but it must have been sometime around the 10th or the 12th of July." Question: "So you only spent about a month providing medical assistance at the Omarska camp?" Answer: "Yes, yes." Having heard this, does this refresh your recollection?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot say exactly how long he was there. He knows it better because it has to do with him directly. I saw that those people, the detainees in the investigation centre, were to have continual health care. Whether it was solved in some other way by the police or the army, or whether he left because he was assigned to some other duty, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: How many times have you been in Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: The first time, one had to see the place where medical aid could be extended, so that is why I went there. So that first time, I saw Professor Cehajic because I knew him and I recognised him. The second time, I was on my way to the investigation centre to help. I was part of the team of the Omarska health centre. But since aid had already been extended -- extended, we were told to go back to our clinic because there was a man wounded who was a Muslim, and we went to help him.
