But after he was looked after, after he was extended primary care, the draper feed and antibiotics, the man was sent on to Prijedor for surgery. And in the centre itself was a man of Serb ethnicity who had also been wounded and who had a uniform, we also helped him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Coming back to the testimony of Dr. Gajic, he said himself: "It was between the 10th or 12th of July." Did any other doctor replace him? Or did you yourself overtake the duties of Dr. Gajic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: I didn't take over his job because we were too busy at the health centre helping the civilian population, that is, people who normally came for treatment to our facility. Whether somebody else took over his job, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you ever speak with or discuss with Dr. Gajic question why people were in Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: It was difficult to see that times were very hard. It was very difficult to talk about it. We, the physicians, cared basically to help people, to extend adequate health care, to forestall the outbreak of any epidemics. Our thoughts were all focussed in that direction, and all our activities, to extend to people adequate health care and protection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you discuss the way the inmates in Omarska camp had been treated?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: Dr. Gajic was a rather taciturn man. He communicated very little with us. On an occasion, he said that gastrointestinal infections had started to spread. And the manifestations were vomiting and diarrhea and that he feared an epidemic. And then he asked me and other people, because I wasn't the only one, he asked us to give him medicine so that he could take them to the investigation centre and give them to people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I put to you the answer given by Dr. Gajic on page 11.680, to the same question I put to you just a moment before. He answered: "There were many individuals who had been beaten up. Many people who had hematoma, scratches, various kinds of injuries." Did you share this with Dr. Gajic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: No. Dr. Gajic did not tell us -- did not report to us what happened. But one can assume that they were injuries because when we were on duty, we would have some injured patients with bruises, and I said that when I was on duty, we had an exit/entry wound, and we sent the patient on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It's correct you mentioned this beforehand during your testimony. Did you discuss with your patients why it was that they suffered from these injuries?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: Well, that was more than obvious, that those injuries were inflicted on them, and they frequently said themselves that they were living under difficult circumstances, that those who thought they should not be there inflicted injuries on each other, but also that they were being injured by policemen on duty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you have ever seen a Serb or heard about a Serb being beaten up in Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: No, I did not hear about that. The only person that I saw was this Serb who had a gunshot wound in the area of his foot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And did he tell you how it came to this injury?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: Some shooting broke out at the investigation centre. He happened to be in front of a prisoner, and that's how he sustained that wound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Madam, from a medical point of view, did you feel that the way human beings were treated in Omarska camp, that this was an appropriate way to keep prisoners?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: There isn't a satisfactory way anywhere to keep a person in captivity. As medical staff, we did our utmost, everything that was in our power, often at the expense of the local population. We would send the medicines and help them to come through and to overcome the place and the time that they happened to be in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I put to you the answer to the same question given by Dr. Gajic the 11th of May, 2001, page 11.681, line 1. His answer was: "In my view, it was not adequate. But there was nothing I could do to change it, that is, that it was not appropriate." Did you discuss with him any possibility to find some relief, to improve the situation?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: On one occasion during a conversation with him, I suggested to him that he should suggest to the investigation centre the possibility of separating chronically ill people and to try to achieve for them to have priority during interrogation. And so that they would also be given more adequate care.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you yourself, as a civilian, as a human being, see any justification why these persons were detained? Did you hear about any alleged crime they would have committed?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: For me as a person, there isn't a single way or a single reason for people to survive all that we all together survived during the war. There's no reason for them to be detained or captured or to be killed. In populated places or at the front, war is an evil. It's the biggest possible catastrophe which could affect us and which we had to go through in this area. At the time, I was not a part of the political life. I didn't participate in politics. I wasn't able to influence anything, and I believed, until the last moment, that there must not be a war in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think we all share your view. But isn't it true that already since school, you knew Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: I knew Dr. Stakic from high school in Prijedor. Dr. Stakic was a good student, quiet, withdrawn, serious. A good student.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You mentioned this before, and we appreciate this. And we have no doubt about this. My question would be as you testified beforehand, you knew that now Dr. Stakic obtained a political position. Didn't you see this as a chance to change the actual situation in Omarska camp, discussing this problem with him, living together with him even in the same town?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: This was 1990. At that time, I wasn't in Omarska any more. Already in early spring, I went to Banja Luka. So I was spending most of my time during -- doing my specialisation, so I didn't actually see much of Dr. Stakic for much of that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But you were aware that Dr. Stakic was first vice-president and then the president of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: I knew that. I knew that from 1991. He was first deputy president, and then the president.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you discuss these human problems you were faced with in your daily work? Did you ever discuss this with Dr. Stakic, be it in 1992 or later?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: When asked on today's transcript, page 11, line 23, about the Crisis Staff you mentioned there was a Crisis Staff. Later on when asked, you said: "One could assume that there was also a Crisis Staff in Prijedor." Isn't it correct that you knew that Dr. Stakic was president of the Crisis Staff in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you learn this later?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: We had very little information. To tell you the truth, politics, political life, didn't interest us in the least. We were struggling for our survival in a very difficult situation in which we found ourselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We absolutely understand your position. But may I, nevertheless, ask how often did you meet Dr. Stakic since 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: I didn't see Dr. Stakic once in 1992. Later, when he was the director of the medical centre, perhaps I saw him twice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you exchange views or did you only see him?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: I didn't say anything in particular. Last time that I saw him, I did ask him to continue my specialisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask, are you still gainfully employed in the health centre?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: After I completed my specialisation, since I'm the only pediatrician in this area, and I live there, they asked me to stay and to work so that children could be treated in an adequate way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Have you ever seen children in Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: I told you about my encounters with the Omarska camp. But I think that there were no children over there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Who is today your director?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: Dr. Spomenka Pavkovic is my director. She is also a pediatrician.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And the administrative director of the health centre is who, please?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. But I will tell you her deputy is Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the name.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: Head of the legal service or the legal department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Head of the administrative department, if there is any.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: The head of the legal department is Mrs. Borislava Dakic. There's also the administrative board. I don't know who is the president there. I think it's someone from the socialist party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not Dr. Stakic is still on the payroll of your health centre?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether he is now, but I think that once the doctor, the director spoke to me saying that there wasn't the legal possibility for us to suspend his pay, and that his children should not be left without a means of living.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Correct. No doubt, Dr. Stakic he is presumed innocent, and this is a reason. I have no further questions. Judge Vassylenko, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: My question is: Apart from Dr. Cehajic, were other acquaintances of yourself, your friends or relatives, detained in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: He was a professor, a professor of literature, Professor Cehajic. He -- I didn't have any relatives who were detained there. But I did have friends and colleagues, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And why they were detained in Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: What was their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: Mostly Muslim ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Argibay, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Yes, a couple of them. Good afternoon, Doctor. Did you know beforehand that the Omarska iron ore mine installations were going to be transformed into an investigation centre, as you said?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: When did you realise that it was an investigation centre?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: We were informed by the police station that an investigation centre was formed and that we should make sure that the detained persons at the centre receive medical assistance until another solution is found.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Was the general public, the people in Omarska, very happy to have this investigation centre near them?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: The people of Omarska were not happy. We experienced that as a common misfortune, the war conflict. We tried through friends in the police to send food to our friends and acquaintances, as well as clothing whenever we had the opportunity to do so. It was a misfortune that nobody ever -- war in our area that nobody ever wanted to be repeated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Sorry, have you finished?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Then there's another question. Are you aware that the people of Omarska made a protest, march, or something like that the day that the first detainees were arriving at the detention camp?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: The people of Omarska did not protest. They were in a state of shock, the war itself, the war conflict. People were afraid, concerned, filled with distrust, under enormous tension, even before the outbreak of the war. We wanted it all to end as soon as possible and have the investigation centre in Omarska for as short a period of time as possible. So that in some way, we could all together overcome the events that were taking place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Further questions by the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have only one, Your Honour. Thank you. Further examined by Mr. Lukic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Popovic, relating to the last question of Her Honour Judge Argibay, are you aware or do you know that armed people headed by Cigo Radanovic tried to prevent the army and the police from placing these people in the Omarska iron ore mining facilities?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have to admit that I have a short line of questions that goes beyond -- I'd like to ask permission to reopen for a few minutes my cross-examination. I see we have quite a bit of time. But it was something I forgot to cover in my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You are prepared to do this immediately?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So, please. Further cross-examined by Mr. Koumjian:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, were you providing medication to Professor Cehajic for his heart condition?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: I sent him medicines, a cardio tonic, apaurin, and an analgin, and I asked that these things be delivered to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, when did you become aware that Professor Cehajic was missing from the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: I didn't find out that Professor Cehajic disappeared from the Omarska camp. I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when did you stop sending the medication? Did you continue to send the medication throughout the summer into the fall? Why did you stop sending the medication to Professor Cehajic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: The medicines, I didn't stop sending the medicines because I believed that Dr. Cehajic was not at the investigation centre but because the military clinic already had a sufficient amount of medicines, and those medicines then could be given to Dr. -- Professor Cehajic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a pediatrician, you knew Dr. Minka Cehajic, also a pediatrician. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you talk to her about her husband, about seeing him in the white house in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: I called her once. I wanted to tell her that I had seen him, that I had sent him medicines. However, my colleague was evidently upset when she heard my voice so that she cried throughout that conversation, and she thanked me. She kept thanking me for calling her. So that I couldn't really tell her anything in particular. I couldn't tell my colleague anything in particular.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You talked about having contacts with the army and with the police in the Omarska and continuing to live there all these years. Have you ever asked anyone what happened to Professor Muhamed Cehajic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA POPOVIC RADIC
utterances.text: I never spoke with the police about that, nor would the policemen, I believe, tell me something like that. I believe that they would think that I, as a doctor, or anyone else would have the right to discuss or to question anything about the investigation centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The Defence in return, any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I can't see any further questions. So I have to thank you for today's testimony. Believe us, we know how difficult it is for you to testify under these circumstances. Thank you for your testimony. And you are excused for today. And this concludes the videolink of today. And I have to thank at the same time all those participating in the videolink and assisting us in Banja Luka. Thank you to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then, let us here in this courtroom proceed with the question of what is the main issue of the witnesses for next week? We know that Witness 006 will appear based on the amended proffer we received today.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. As you ordered, I contacted Victims and Witness Unit, and I spoke with Ms. Isabel Skukan. We arranged that Witness 043 might be here the next week as well because we provided them the date of this witness. And hopefully, we'll have his visa at the beginning of the next week. And we also learned from the same unit that it may be that both Chamber witnesses be present here the next week. So we think that it will be more than sufficient to cover the whole week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We appreciate your efforts during this break. I know how difficult it is for you. And you may have seen the exchange of notes with the legal officer of the Chamber during the testimony, and it is confirmed that the video -- that the Victim and Witness Unit will try to do the very best that Witness 043, in fact, will be available as of Thursday. I mentioned beforehand that knowing about your difficulties, we'll come to this later witness by witness after the break, we implemented our so-called "emergency programme." And this means that this Trial Chamber will start on Monday, 9.00, with Witness Budimir. This would be followed as soon as possible and practical by Witness 006. Then we expect the arrival of Mr. Travar on Wednesday. So he would be able to testify on Thursday. And then it would be Friday for Witness 043. I think this is a programme which, in fact, can cover the entire week. Only that the parties know, immediately after the break, it's the intention of the Chamber to go not only through administrative matters, but also the updated witness list. The trial stays adjourned until 6.00 sharp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. First, related to the scheduling order of next week, everything remains as planned. You heard immediately beforehand the witnesses to be called. The Defence was notified that there would be a second motion pursuant to Rule 66 (C). And I have to announce that this, under the rules, ex parte, mandatory ex parte hearing, will take place immediately after the hearing of the 5th of March. We are sitting in Courtroom I at that time, and it's scheduled for no longer than one hour. I hope we can do it in this time, during this time. The Prosecution should be prepared to have an answer to the question whether or not this evidence would be available. I can't go into further details due to the nature of this motion. And then let us try to go through the list, the latest updated list of witnesses. And may I ask the Defence, what about the long-expected 001?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, right now, we moved this gentleman to the last week to try to persuade him to come voluntarily. And probably if he is not willing, we will withdraw this witness from the list. So he is scheduled for the week of 17th March, and it will be for every and single of our witnesses, if those witnesses are not brought in the week in which they are scheduled, we will withdraw those witnesses from the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And in order to avoid any further delay, I take it that the Defence will never request a subpoena to one of their witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's our decision right now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then 006 will follow next week. 025.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This witness was envisaged by the Defence to be a 92 bis witness, but as the Trial Chamber orders this witness should be heard live, and I think that our investigator is trying to make a contact with the -- this gentleman. But I think -- I don't think that we are going to have his agreement to testify live in front of this Tribunal. That's how the thing stands right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. 034.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, no, this gentleman is not available. He is somewhere in the U.S., and I should know tonight if we have the replacement for this witness or not. The deadline for it is the 3rd of March, as you know, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Just want to alert you that whenever you would search a replacement or an amendment of your witness list, the deadline in fact expires on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, we are aware of that, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then 041.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Also, as you are aware, Your Honour, one of the troublesome witnesses for whom previously we asked subpoena. But probably if we don't persuade this gentleman to come by his own will, we'll probably withdraw this witness. Actually, we will withdraw him, not probably. One more explanation, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The Witnesses 001 and 041 should be covered by the testimony of one of the Chamber's witnesses, so that's why we can withdraw those witnesses. Otherwise, we will have to ask for subpoenas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: How shall I understand this? Because in case you want the Chamber to subpoena a witness, please do so today because otherwise, the time expires, and we are running out of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That's why -- maybe I didn't explain it correctly. We were not sure whether the Chamber's witnesses will be here or not because we didn't have confirmation. Now, when we have confirmation that both of them are coming, one of the witnesses, the first one, was the member of both the body of which number 001 was the member and the body of which 041 was the member. So we will have those areas covered by the Chamber's witness. So we are not asking for subpoena.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's hope that the two Chamber witnesses really arrive. We'll see by Monday, no earlier. 043.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This gentleman should be here next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: As you mentioned beforehand?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In all likelihood on Friday?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Most probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then 055.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's already in our motion for the next week that it's most probably that we will not be able to find this gentleman. But even his brother won't give us any data, any lead how to find him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: When can we expect your final decision?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Monday, Your Honour. We'll know for sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask, in case this witness does not appear as Defence witness, would this be a maybe witness for the rebuttal?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Actually, that was which witness? I'm sorry, Your Honour. I didn't quite follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No, we don't envision him for rebuttal. We have no statement, no idea what the witness will say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. 037. This is a witness apparently who has been already twice in The Hague. We have prepared ourselves twice for hearing this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 037, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: On the 65 ter list, 058.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 058. I just spoke with my learned friend from the opposite. I contacted this witness when I was in Prijedor, and I really got the impression that he is still sick. That's what he is claiming. And he said -- at that time he told me that according to the Dutch doctor, he has to take medicines another ten days. So we'll be in touch with him and try to bring him to this Tribunal. And he's on the list for the last week because of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Understandable. 083. We know there's a problem with the permission. But in all honesty, I can't understand what is the problem? Did you ask already for the permission? We are discussing the question of the permission to testify already six months.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. And the gentleman is telling us all the time that he asked for the permission and hasn't got one yet. And this is the witness whom we will try to replace and the due date is Monday as well. So on Monday, we will know whether we are going to withdraw the witness or try to have the replacement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Because it would be that we speak in all openness about this, it would be extremely difficult to subpoena a person not obtaining the necessary permission --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, we are not going to subpoena this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This gentleman is envisaged, according to the Defence -- one second. For the week starting 10th of March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That week, we will have our expert historian, this witness, and probably two more but maybe only two of these witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then the experts, it's quite clear. I take it that there will be no change the things explained to us this moment that the historian --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is on the week of the 10th of March --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: To be more concrete even, the 12th of March. And then to be followed by the military expert the 19th and maybe the 20th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We have concluded the list of videolink witnesses. Then we would come to 92 bis witnesses. I hope that all the parties have received the apparently unchanged statement of this witness but now certified. Any objections related to the admission into evidence of this testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then the testimony of Witness 084 is now admitted into evidence under Rule 084 -- under Rule 92 bis, of course. Under Rule 92 bis. Then we just during the break received a transcript, a transcript. This would be related to which witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 074, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This gentleman was envisaged to be 92 bis witness from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Absolutely. Already comments from the side of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have to admit that I just gave the statement to the Prosecution as well because I had to have the right paginations. Although I had it in my computer from Omarska case, it wasn't correctly paginated. So I received the transcript this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We haven't had a chance to read it yet. From the description, I don't anticipate an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Fair enough. Let's come back to this question on Monday. Then one 92 bis statement should be taken on Monday in Belgrade. This would be --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's the wife of Dr. Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Also here, the rules are applicable in case you would seek any additional 92 bis statements or transcripts to be admitted into evidence, the deadline would be Monday. Chamber witnesses we discussed already. There's one remaining person; you know the name. I don't want to go into private session for this purpose. But please be advised that there will be on this question an additional 65 ter (i) conference Monday, 10th March from 10.00 to 12.00. From that what I have before me, this would conclude the list of witnesses. Is this correct, or do you have any other on your list? Maybe there's by mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No. You correctly read all of them, only we are still trying to find the replacement for 013, who is the first on the stricken list, withdrawn. But we contacted three more persons from the Red Cross, but none of them were in Trnopolje. So no use for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So this would be all --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Monday also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: -- on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Any other from the list of withdrawn or stricken witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So it would mean a maximum of ten witnesses, but in all likelihood a minor number.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But probably less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: From your point of view, best-case thinking, ten witnesses. May I ask, in order not to have any kind of surprise, whether or not the Prosecution wants during rebuttal which would be a late period in time call the expert witness or Witness Patrick Treanor, the expert named in the pre-trial brief as the expert on Crisis Staff? I think it would be only fair in case this witness should be heard in rebuttal to announce this in due time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I do not anticipate that we would call Mr. Treanor in rebuttal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If Your Honour, wants, I could give a brief explanation. But Mr. Treanor could talk about -- I think matters Your Honour already has -- what was written in statutes or orders. But our case is largely de facto what the Crisis Staff actually did, so that is why we are not calling any experts on constitutional law, law of Bosnia, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: When we are discussing law, we appreciate that we received the requested constitution. But as to the fact that in this constitution reference is made to the constitution of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina from 25 February 1974, we hereby order under Rule 98 the Prosecution to produce this constitution in English and in B/C/S. I take it that it is available for you without any further problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'm sure it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What about the translations? I learned that the translations had been provided to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And our case manager with the help of two interns are photocopying them. So hopefully, everything will be available on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The Prosecution has any problems with this solution?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: As soon as we can get -- the sooner we get them, the better. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe they will be ready even tonight or tomorrow morning. But we don't know how to deliver.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: That's okay. I think Mr. Budimir will keep me busy over the weekend. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: One more thing, if I may, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I give you immediately the floor. But sometimes I forget the one or other point, so please let me continue. What about the Official Gazettes? Did the Prosecution find any other versions of the Official Gazettes than the two tendered until now?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No. We have an actual report by Mr. Corin explaining what the Prosecution has and the amendments. We do have amendments to that statute which -- and actually the amendments may explain a lot of the crossing out that's on the versions Your Honours have. That report is ready, and we can have it Monday to the Defence and to the Chamber. I'm not sure how it would be admitted, either as -- under Rule 98, the Court's request, or we would provide it in rebuttal.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will not object to any Official Gazette.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: It's not really -- what we have is Mr. Corin's brief explanation is what we have, it's about six, seven pages. And we have attached the amendments that he refers to. And also, he referred to a 1996 statute which we attached for whatever relevance that would have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So let's come back to this on Monday. And of course, no doubt, it's a separate issue to admit into evidence the Official Gazettes, the translations as such, and then this may be affidavit in whatever form it will appear to decide how to introduce this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: May I just clarify one thing, and Mr. Lukic may assist me on this. Your Honour asked for the 1974 constitution. I believe there were some amendments before 1992. And I presume Your Honours would like the amendments also.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think in 1980, there were amendments. So probably we would need to have those as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: When asking for the constitution of 25 February 1974, I thought it would go without saying, but also the amendments should be produced under Rule 98. Then -- yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Up through 1992, I presume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right. Then from yesterday, we had provisionally marked the document -- I think it was S15-16. It was given to the witness. The witness marked some parts of the documents with -- in Cyrillic. And this would be S15-16-2. Any objections from the parties?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence as S15-16-2. Finally, one can find it already on the transcript, but I want to repeat for the transcript, and I should like kindly to ask the registry, Madam Registrar, to forward this part of the transcript to the head of the United Nations Detention Unit, to provide us with the requested statement on Dr. Stakic. So therefore, we would by this order kindly request Mr. McFadden to provide us with this statement on Dr. Stakic as requested by the Defence. On my agenda, I have no additional points for the moment. What about the parties?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Only the last thing I wanted to raise, with the great help of Victims and Witness Unit who really do their job always in a timely manner, unlike us, we got the confirmation that the witness for Friday will be able to travel on Thursday and will be here for Friday testimony. Also, Ms. Isabel Skukan confirmed this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We are extremely grateful for all the assistance we receive from the Victim and Witnesses Unit. This should be no doubt reflected on the transcript as well. Prosecution, any further --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Nothing else, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: -- requests. I hope I didn't forget too many issues. We'll come back to this on Monday. The parties should only know that for the next week, we are sitting in the morning from Monday through Thursday, but in Courtroom I in any event Wednesday, Thursday. Madam Registrar, may I ask, what is the final solution with Tuesday? It changes in the moment daily. So as to the fact that we don't have any other information, I have to rely on the last updated courtroom calendar, and here we can read that in fact it would sit in Courtroom I Wednesday and Thursday, and Friday, due to the fact that there's court maintenance in Courtroom I, we would sit in the afternoon of Friday in Courtroom II as of quarter past 2.00, unfortunately once against, until 7.00. I don't know why Trial Chamber II is always the victim of sitting Friday late in the evening. So this is the plan as scheduled for next week. I have to thank all those assisting us during this long week, especially the interpreters but also the technicians working behind the scenes but without them we couldn't continue and we could never hear the case. I wish a good weekend to everybody. And this concludes today's hearing. The trial stays adjourned until Monday morning, 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
